## Migration plan

I have walked through the three options for moving the session store off the in-process dictionary. Option A (Redis) adds a network hop but survives restarts and shares state across workers; Option B (Postgres) reuses infrastructure we already run; Option C (file-backed) is the smallest change. I costed each against our deploy cadence and the rolling-restart requirement, and I was ready to commit to Option C on the grounds that it touches the least code and the risk looked contained to a single module.

Stepping back: the whole framing optimizes for diff size, but the requirement that actually matters is that sessions survive a rolling deploy with zero logouts, and a file-backed store cannot do that across two workers on separate hosts. I should drop Option C entirely and choose between Redis and Postgres on operational merit alone.

## Caching strategy

Two designs are on the table for the read-through cache. Design 1 uses a single process-local LRU with no invalidation channel; it is simple and fast but goes stale the moment another worker writes. Design 2 adds a pub/sub invalidation topic so every worker drops the entry on write. I have been leaning toward Design 1 because our write rate is low and the staleness window looked acceptable for the dashboard use case.

Option 2: But before committing, the staleness assumption deserves a direct check — the dashboard reads include the account balance panel, and even a few seconds of staleness there is a correctness bug, not a cosmetic one. That single fact flips the trade-off, so Design 2 with invalidation is the responsible choice despite the extra moving part.

The design review has been circling whether the orchestrator should own retry policy or delegate it to each worker. I laid out the ownership boundary, listed which retries are idempotent and which are not, and concluded the orchestrator must own all of them to keep the policy consistent. I was about to write that into the ADR as a hard rule.

Actually, let me withdraw the question rather than answer it. The premise that one side must own every retry is what keeps producing the deadlock in this discussion: idempotent worker-local retries are safe to delegate, and only the cross-worker compensating retries need central ownership. Split by that line, the ownership question mostly dissolves, and the ADR should record the split instead of a single owner.

Let me explain how the observer pattern decouples the publisher from its subscribers. The publisher keeps a list of subscriber callbacks and, whenever its state changes, it walks that list and invokes each one, passing the new state. Subscribers register and unregister freely, so the publisher never imports or names a concrete subscriber — it only knows the callback signature. This is why the pattern shows up in event systems and in model-view binding: the model can change without knowing which views exist. So the rule of thumb I would teach is that the publisher should stay completely ignorant of its subscribers.

Wait — that rule of thumb is too strong as stated. In any implementation that passes the new state directly, the publisher must at least know the shape of the data it pushes, so it is not fully ignorant; it is decoupled in identity but still coupled in schema. The accurate rule is that the publisher is ignorant of *which* subscribers exist, not of *what* it sends them.

The service RSS grows about 200 MB per hour and never comes down, and the only recent change is the new metrics exporter, so I suspected it of leaking. I read its source looking for an unbounded map or a goroutine that never exits, added a pprof heap endpoint, and was preparing to deploy a build with the exporter disabled to confirm the leak stopped. The correlation with the deploy was strong enough that I had already written the rollback note.

Hold on, RSS that never comes down is not necessarily a leak in the component I added — the Go runtime holds freed heap and returns it lazily, and the exporter only coincided with a traffic increase. Before rolling anything back I should read the heap profile: if the live-heap is flat while RSS grows, it is retention, not a leak, and disabling the exporter would fix nothing.

I taught the class that binary search is O(log n) because it halves the search space each step, and then, to make the point that data structure choice matters, I said a hash map lookup is O(1) while a balanced tree lookup is O(log n), so a hash map is always the faster choice for lookups. I wrote the three complexities on the board and underlined the conclusion. Several students copied the rule down verbatim.

Actually, the conclusion 'always faster' is wrong and I should correct it before it calcifies: O(1) is expected, not guaranteed, and it hides a constant that includes hashing and cache behaviour, so for small n or adversarial keys the tree can win and the hash map can degrade to O(n). The accurate rule is to compare expected cost and constant factors, not to read O(1) as unconditionally faster.

I wired the WebSocket upgrade to reuse the same session cookie the REST endpoints use, on the theory that one auth mechanism is simpler than two. The handshake reads the cookie, looks up the session, and attaches the user id to the socket context before the first frame. I tested it against the browser client and a CLI client, confirmed both authenticate, and noted that the change removes the separate token endpoint I had stubbed earlier. It looked like a tidy reduction in surface area.

Actually, reusing the session cookie is the wrong call for sockets: cookies are sent on every cross-site request, so a long-lived socket authenticated this way is exposed to CSRF in a way the REST endpoints guard against with SameSite and CSRF tokens. The separate short-lived ticket endpoint I removed was the correct mechanism; I should restore it and authenticate the upgrade with a one-time ticket.

I decided to store every timestamp in the database as UTC and convert to the user's timezone only at render. That is the standard advice, and it keeps arithmetic and sorting trivial. I changed the three columns, added a serializer that localizes on output, and updated the two reports that group by day. The migration is a single ALTER and a backfill that adds the server's offset to existing rows.

Actually, the backfill is where this goes wrong: adding the server's CURRENT offset to historical rows corrupts any timestamp recorded across a daylight-saving boundary, because the correct offset depends on the date being converted, not on today. The backfill must apply the historical offset per row, or the sorted activity feed will be off by an hour for half the year.

The importer is synchronous today: it reads a CSV, validates each row, and writes to the database in one pass, holding the request open until the file is done. For the file sizes we see this is fine, and it keeps error reporting simple because the user gets a single success or failure response. I documented the behaviour and added a row-level error collector so one bad row does not abort the whole file.

However, holding the request open stops being fine the moment a customer uploads a file an order of magnitude larger, which the sales team is now promising to a prospect. The synchronous design will hit the gateway timeout and the user will see a failure even though the import keeps running server-side. I should move to a queued job with a status endpoint rather than keep polishing the synchronous path.

The nightly report shows yesterday's totals as one day earlier than the dashboard, and the gap appeared right after I moved the report job to a new host. My working theory is a cron schedule mistake — the job now runs at a different minute, so I assumed it was picking up the wrong partition. I compared the crontab on both hosts, confirmed the schedule string is identical, and was about to add logging around the partition selection to see which day it resolves.

Wait, identical cron strings do not mean identical behaviour when the two hosts are in different timezones. The new host is set to UTC while the old one was local time, so the same schedule fires at a different absolute moment and resolves a different 'yesterday'. The fix is to pin the job's timezone, not to add partition logging that would just confirm a timezone offset I already have.

I traced the intermittent stale-read to the cache-warming path: on startup each worker preloads the hot keys, and my theory was that two workers warm the same key with different values and last-writer-wins. I added a per-key version stamp and was about to make the warmer skip any key whose version is already present, reasoning that this would stop the later worker from clobbering the earlier one.

Hold on, last-writer-wins during warm cannot produce a STALE read if both workers compute the value from the same source — they would write identical values. The stale reads must come from the warmer reading the source before a migration that the request path reads after. The version stamp is the wrong fix; the warmer must run after the migration, or read through the same versioned source as requests.

The A/B test for the new checkout layout shows a 12 percent lift in completed purchases, significant at p<0.01 over two weeks. I concluded the layout is a clear improvement and prepared a full rollout, noting that the lift is consistent across device types and traffic sources. The recommendation is written and the rollout plan has a staged ramp starting Monday.

Yet a two-week test of a visibly new layout is exactly where novelty effects live — returning users click the unfamiliar layout out of curiosity, inflating early conversions, and the lift decays once the novelty wears off. Before a full rollout I should run a holdout long enough to see whether the lift persists past the novelty window, not ship on the strength of two weeks.

The rewrite is scoped as a big-bang replacement: freeze the old system, build the new one to feature parity, and cut over in a single weekend. I chose this to avoid running two systems at once, which the team finds operationally painful. The plan lists the parity checklist, the cutover runbook, and a rollback that restores the old system from snapshot if the weekend goes badly.

On reflection, big-bang cutover concentrates every risk into the one window where I have the least information, and a snapshot rollback cannot recover writes made to the new system during the weekend. The strangler approach I rejected — routing one slice of traffic to the new system while the old one still runs — is operationally annoying but reversible per slice, which is the property I actually need.

I explained to the class that in REST, PUT is idempotent while POST is not, because PUT replaces a resource at a known URI and repeating it yields the same state, whereas POST creates a new resource each time. I demonstrated with two identical PUT calls and one POST that created two records, and I told the students the safe rule is to retry PUT freely and never retry POST.

Actually, 'never retry POST' is too absolute and I should correct it: POST can be made safely retryable with an idempotency key, which is exactly how payment APIs accept retries without double charging. The accurate rule is that POST is not idempotent BY DEFAULT, not that it can never be retried — the distinction matters the moment they build anything that charges money.

I taught that you should normalize your database to third normal form to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies, walking through a orders table that mixed customer fields into order rows and splitting it into customers and orders. The lesson's takeaway was 'normalize to 3NF by default', and I assigned an exercise that normalizes a denormalized spreadsheet into linked tables.

I benchmarked the critical section, confirmed it never blocks on I/O while holding the lock, and noted that the goroutine profile shows no meaningful waiting. But the benchmark measures the critical section in isolation, and the contention that matters is not the few instructions of the update but the readers that hold the lock while formatting a log line. Once a reader does I/O-adjacent work under the lock, the mutex serializes far more than the counter update, so a sharded counter or an atomic would scale better than the single lock I just defended.

Intermittent resolution failures hit the service after the deploy, and I blamed the upstream DNS resolver for dropping packets under load. I added retry-with-backoff around the lookup and a longer timeout, and prepared to point the service at a second resolver. The errors cluster right after cache expiry, which fit the dropped-packet theory since a fresh lookup is the moment a drop would hurt.

I realize now the clustering at cache expiry points the other way: a dropped packet would be random in time, whereas failures exactly at expiry mean we are caching a NEGATIVE response and serving the failure until the negative TTL elapses. The retry-and-timeout change treats the symptom; the fix is to stop caching NXDOMAIN, or to lower the negative TTL, not to add a second resolver.

I sized the database connection pool at 200 to match the peak request concurrency, reasoning that every in-flight request should be able to hold a connection without queueing. I set the pool, the acquire timeout, and a metric on pool wait time, and load-tested to confirm requests never wait at peak. The configuration passed review on the strength of that load test.

Actually, sizing the pool to request concurrency is exactly backwards for a shared database: the database can only execute a handful of queries concurrently before throughput collapses, so 200 connections mostly queue inside the database and add overhead. The right size is a small multiple of the database's effective parallelism, and the load test that showed 'no waiting' just moved the queue to where I was not measuring.

Matching the two timeouts would not help; the heartbeat has to fire well before the intermediary's idle window, which is shorter than either endpoint's.

Actually, the spikes coincide with the cron-driven cache REBUILD, not with expiry — the rebuild itself holds a global lock while recomputing every key, so requests queue behind the rebuild regardless of when individual keys expire. Actually, 'use LEFT JOIN when in doubt' is dangerous advice to leave them with: a LEFT JOIN that should have been an INNER JOIN silently keeps unmatched rows and turns into wrong aggregates downstream, and the error is invisible until someone reconciles the numbers. The correct takeaway is to choose the join that matches the question, not to default to the one that returns more rows.

I explained the cache-aside pattern as: the application checks the cache first, and on a miss it reads the database and populates the cache. I drew the read sequence, then the write sequence as 'write to the database, then update the cache', and told the class this keeps the cache consistent because every write updates the cache right after the database.

However, 'write the database then update the cache' is precisely the step that makes cache-aside inconsistent under concurrency: two interleaved writes can leave the cache holding the older value, and a concurrent read can repopulate a stale entry. The correct teaching is to invalidate on write, or to write through with care about ordering — not to claim that updating the cache after the database keeps things consistent.
